strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the critical modality reasoning gap in Speech LLMs with clear articulation of why existing input-side and output-side approaches are insufficient

Technically sound design combining complementary dense rewards (representation alignment for internal drift + behavior alignment for output consistency) with clever modality-specific normalization to prevent negative advantage skewing

Strong empirical results achieving 98.89-100.45% MRR on tested benchmarks and outperforming diverse baselines (SALAD, DeSTA, AlignChat, KD, cascaded systems) while improving both audio and text accuracy

Comprehensive experimental validation with thoughtful ablations (Table 2), layer sensitivity analysis revealing middle-layer criticality, and representation drift analysis (Figure 3) demonstrating genuine alignment
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, and promise to release code; clear writing and well-structured presentation
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope significantly undermines generalization claims: (1) only 7B scale—unclear how representation/behavior alignment scales to 13B+ models where architectural dynamics differ; (2) only two similar multiple-choice QA benchmarks—no evaluation on mathematical reasoning, code generation, or open-ended generation; (3) all speech is synthesized—no evaluation on natural speech with accent/noise variability, severely limiting practical applicability

Circular reference in text branch methodology: text completions serve as reference targets but are simultaneously updated during training (Eq. 2), creating a moving-target problem. No analysis of whether this 'co-evolution' is necessary or if frozen text references would suffice. This confounds the interpretation of alignment

Reward design lacks principled justification: (1) weights α=1.0, β=1.0 appear arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; (2) representation alignment uses simple mean cosine similarity—more sophisticated metrics unexplored; (3) behavior alignment depends on external embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B) without exploring sensitivity to embedding choice; (4) critical failure mode unaddressed: when no correct text completion exists in batch, both Rrep and Rbeh fall to 0, potentially crippling effectiveness on harder problems

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance testing on main results (Table 1); single runs reported; with multiple-choice accuracy, differences may not be significant. Only Figure 3 includes confidence intervals, making it unclear whether improvements are statistically meaningful

Critical missing ablations: no isolated ablation of modality-specific normalization; no sensitivity analysis for α, β, group size G; no comparison of different embedding models; no analysis of performance when batches contain no correct text completions; no evaluation at multiple random seeds

Fundamental limitation of synthetic speech undermines real-world applicability: all training and evaluation uses synthesized speech (CosyVoice2, openaudio-s1-mini). Unknown how method performs on natural speech with speaker variability, accents, background noise, or speech artifacts—critical for practical deployment

Scale limitation at submission time: 7B-only evaluation in 2026 is limiting given trends toward 13B+ models. Architectural and optimization dynamics may differ significantly at larger scales, making extrapolation unreliable

MRR metric interpretation problem: MRR = audio_accuracy / text_accuracy × 100%. When text accuracy improves during training (76.17%→78.56%), computing MRR against changing denominator conflates audio alignment improvements with base model capability improvements, making absolute gains ambiguous

Incomplete methodological transparency: (1) text-speech interleaving during optimization not clearly specified; (2) cascaded baseline uses unspecified ASR (Whisper-large-v3) without justifying it's strongest available; (3) xFinder answer extraction sensitivity unexplored; (4) two different training frameworks used (ms-swift vs. HuggingFace TRL) without justification

Narrow task evaluation and limited real-world relevance: evaluation restricted to multiple-choice QA format. No evaluation on reasoning modalities mentioned in motivation (mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning in natural interaction patterns), limiting claims about closing reasoning gaps more broadly

strengths: Well-motivated problem: The modality reasoning gap is a genuine and important challenge in Speech LLMs with clear articulation of why existing input-side and output-side approaches are insufficient
Thoughtful technical contributions: Asymmetric reward design and modality-specific normalization elegantly address practical challenges in aligning speech and text reasoning
Comprehensive experimental ablations: Table 2, Figure 2, and Figure 3 provide useful component analysis, layer sensitivity studies, and representation alignment investigations
Strong empirical results on targeted benchmarks: Achieves near 100% MRR on MMSU and OBQA, outperforming multiple baselines (SALAD, DeSTA, MiniCPM-o)
Reproducibility commitments: Detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, and promised code/dataset release in appendices
weaknesses: Critical scope limitations: Evaluation restricted to 7B scale only; unclear if method scales to 13B/70B+ models. Two QA benchmarks insufficient to claim general reasoning gap solution. Uses only synthesized speech (WER <10% filtered)—generalization to natural speech completely unvalidated

Unexplained text performance paradox: Text accuracy improves (78.39%→83.82% for Phi-4-MM) during speech RL training, contradicting the claimed alignment mechanism. This suggests potential confounds or that improvements stem from training dynamics rather than alignment

Weak theoretical foundation: Layer-wise cosine similarity choice unjustified; representational drift diagnosis relies on correlation not causation; no ablation on α=β=1.0 weights or embedding model choice

Methodological concerns: Missing baseline of pure text training or balanced text+speech; representation reward degrades to 0 when no correct text reference available; text completions assumed correct despite potential errors propagating through alignment signal

Incomplete causal analysis: Figure 3 shows similarities change but doesn't prove this *causes* reasoning improvement; no error analysis of speech-specific failures; unchanged WER suggests acoustic encoder unoptimized; gap origin (encoding vs. projection vs. reasoning) unidentified

Cascaded baseline unfairness: Comparison between different ASR systems (Whisper-large-v3 vs. Speech LLM encoder) and model families doesn't isolate alignment contribution; end-to-end advantage could stem from avoiding ASR errors

Synthesized speech-only training is fundamental limitation: TTS removes natural speech challenges (noise, accents, prosody variation); transferability to real-world speech unknown and critical for practical applications

Limited novelty: RL for alignment established in literature; combining representation+behavior losses is straightforward; main contributions (asymmetric rewards, modality normalization) are incremental engineering choices without theoretical grounding

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of the modality reasoning gap and limitations of prior approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablations, layer sensitivity analysis, and teacher-forcing validation across two models

Strong empirical results achieving near-complete modality recovery (MRR ≥ 98.89%) and state-of-the-art performance among 7B models, outperforming strong baselines substantially (e.g., 76.84% vs 66.30% SALAD on Qwen2.5)
Technically sound approach combining complementary alignment signals with clever modality-specific normalization to prevent negative advantages
Notable finding that gains improve rather than trade-off text performance, suggesting genuine cross-modal knowledge transfer
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and promise to release code and datasets
Clear presentation with informative visualizations and well-reasoned motivation for why prior input-side and output-side methods are insufficient
weaknesses: Evaluation limited to 7B-scale models only; scaling behavior to 13B, 70B, or larger models remains unknown, limiting confidence in generalizability

Training and evaluation exclusively on synthetic speech (TTS-generated) with no natural speech evaluation; practical applicability to real speech with accent variation, background noise, and speaker characteristics unclear
Narrow task scope confined to two multiple-choice QA benchmarks (MMSU, OBQA); generalization to other reasoning domains (math, coding, logical reasoning) and non-QA tasks undemonstrated
Single-turn reasoning only; multi-turn dialogue and interactive speech reasoning not addressed despite being important Speech LLM use cases

Fundamental architecture relies entirely on text-conditioned completions as alignment references, preventing capture of paralinguistic cues (emotion, prosody, intent) that exist only in speech—acknowledged but unresolved
Incremental technical novelty: primarily applies existing GRPO framework with domain-specific reward engineering; modality-specific normalization appears ad-hoc rather than principled
Incomplete baseline comparisons: SSR and some other recent methods mentioned but absent from results; anonymous submissions make concurrent-vs-prior work unclear
Missing ablations on key design choices: no sensitivity analysis on α and β weights (fixed at 1.0), no evaluation of embedding model alternatives, no exploration of why middle layers are optimal
No failure case analysis: which reasoning patterns still struggle? What explains remaining 4% absolute gap between audio (79.80%) and text (83.82%) on Phi-4-MM OBQA?
MRR metric uses non-ceiling text performance as denominator (e.g., 76.17% for Qwen2.5); 100% recovery to a below-ceiling baseline is less meaningful than achieving absolute performance ceiling
Computational cost context missing: 55/35-hour training times mentioned but not compared to baselines; inference efficiency implications unclear
Reproducibility partially limited: Phi-4-MM-7B is internal model; only Qwen2.5-Omni is fully externally reproducible
Data source unexplored: UnifiedQA may not be optimally suited for speech reasoning; no ablation on data composition impact on results

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear diagnosis of why existing approaches (adapter tuning, knowledge distillation) are insufficient; articulates exposure bias and representation drift issues compellingly

Sound technical approach: asymmetric reward design elegantly provides dense signals even when task accuracy is zero, avoiding sparse-reward failure modes; modality-specific normalization addresses imbalanced rewards without architectural changes

Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extensive ablations (Table 2, 4.4) clearly demonstrating contribution of each component; layer-wise analysis (Figure 2, Section 5.1) provides interpretable evidence of representational drift mitigation

Strong empirical results: achieves MRR ≥98.89% on Qwen2.5-Omni and 100.45% on Phi-4-MM, substantially exceeding baselines; text performance improves alongside speech (78.56% vs 76.17%), demonstrating no catastrophic forgetting

Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, baseline descriptions, implementation frameworks specified; promises code/dataset release; efficiency analysis (4.4% overhead) with GPU hours provided
Thorough analysis including per-domain breakdown (Table 7), sensitivity to layer groups (Figure 3), generalization to real speech (SD-QA), and qualitative examples (Tables 9-10) supporting key claims
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging unknown behavior at other scales and multi-turn reasoning
weaknesses: Critical limitation: evaluation restricted to 7B scale only with no experiments at 3B or 13B; severely limits claims of broad applicability and state-of-the-art status for a 2026 venue submission

Stage-dependent reward design (Section 5.3) shows Phi-4-MM benefits from Rrep while Qwen2.5-Omni over-regularizes and requires Rbeh-only configuration, suggesting method requires per-model tuning and raises generalization concerns

Training exclusively on high-quality synthetic speech with 10% WER filtering; generalization to real speech marginal (Table 4: 41.95% audio vs 44.30% text); no robustness analysis for background noise, accents, or speech degradation

Mean-pooling of hidden states (Eq. 4) discards sequential structure within reasoning spans; no justification for why this coarse mechanism is appropriate vs alternatives like attention-weighted or token-level alignment

Representation alignment fallback (Rrep=0 when no correct text completion available) occurs 5.9-10.7% of time, risking training instability; behavior alignment similarly requires correct text references, limiting applicability to speech-first scenarios

Evaluation limited to multiple-choice QA tasks (MMSU, OBQA); no free-form generation, open-ended reasoning, or multi-turn dialogue; acknowledged limitation but represents substantial scope restriction

Moderate conceptual novelty: individual components (cosine similarity, semantic embeddings, GRPO) well-established; main contribution is combining them with asymmetric on-policy rewards, useful but incremental engineering contribution

Layer-wise analysis uses teacher forcing (Appendix E), not reflecting true online free-generation dynamics where speech and text may diverge earlier; hyperparameters (α, β, λ) appear fixed without sensitivity ablations
